newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Rio shantytown drug wars close down schools.
newsitem.headline: Rio shantytown drug wars close down schools.

text.p: Shootouts between drug traffickers in shantytowns in the north of Rio de Janeiro closed down four schools, a city education department official said on Friday.

"We decided to close four schools yesterday," said education coordinator Sonia Mograbi. "Parents stopped sending their children to school after heavy gun fights raged overnight. There is always the worry that the school might be hit by stray bullets."
The schools in the Agua Santa suburb of Rio are located in between two hilltop shantytowns where rival drug gangs have been battling since the weekend for the control of drug sales points.
Mograbi said police had calmed the situation and the 3,000 students affected by the school closure returned to their lessons on Friday, but the violence could flare up again at any time.

Rio de Janeiro's school for children of French expatriates, the Liceu Moliere, located in the middle-class neighbourhood of Laranjeiras in the south of the city, faced similar problems and was considering a move to somewhere else.
Frequent gun battles in a nearby shantytown and the discovery of three bodies near the school's entrance shot dead by drug gangs have prompted the school to look at relocating.

"Our hope was that the state government would control the situation in the shantytown, but police operations are not resolving the problem. The solution is to move out of Pereira da Silva Street," Michel Oyharcabal, president of the Franco-Brazilian Society for Education, told Jornal do Brasil.
In a first move to protect its students, the Liceu Moliere installed bullet proof glass and steel plates in some of the walls and windows in recent months.
Even residents in Rio de Janeiro's most prosperous neighbourhoods often cannot escape the violence bred in the shantytowns given the city's geography.
The layout of Rio resembles a leopard skin with shantytowns dotting the landscape and overlooking the city as they perch atop Rio's many hillsides.

Almost every week the newspapers tell the story of another innocent bystander being injured or killed by a stray bullet as the city's criminals arm themselves with evermore sophisticated weapons in their hilltop fiefdoms.
